one_liner: Header-only C++ runtime expression parser/evaluator; evaluates pre-compiled expressions about 2-4x faster than muparser 2.2.4.
what_it_does: ExprTk parses a string such as 'sqrt(1 - (3 / x^2))' at run time into an expression tree bound by reference to C++ variables registered in a symbol_table, then evaluates it repeatedly with expression.value(). The language goes well beyond arithmetic: scalars, vectors, strings, if/switch, loops, user-defined C++ functions, composited functions and numerical integration/differentiation. It is not an API drop-in for muparser (different symbol_table/parser/expression objects and syntax extensions), though plain arithmetic expressions mostly parse the same.
how_it_is_fast: It is a tree-walking interpreter, not a JIT and not SIMD: the gain comes from compile-time work. The parser does constant folding, strength reduction and dead-code elimination, rewrites integer powers into multiplication chains (cardinal pow optimisation), and synthesises operand-type-specialised node templates (vov/voc/cov nodes and fused T0oT1oT2 / T0oT1oT2oT3 three- and four-operand nodes with variable or constant slots baked in as template parameters), so common shapes like 'a*x+b' become one virtual call instead of a small subtree. Vector operations use an 8-way (or 4-way) manually unrolled loop.
when_to_use: Parse-once, evaluate-many workloads: user-entered formulas, config-driven transforms, spreadsheet-like columns, simulation parameters evaluated millions of times
You need double (or float, long double, MPFR) precision with results that match native C++ arithmetic closely; precision is the library's stated first priority
Expressions need more than arithmetic: conditionals, loops, string predicates, vectors, or calls back into C++ functions
Portable builds on any compiler down to C++98 (the header reports min_cpp 199711L) without third-party dependencies or a JIT
when_not_to_use: Compile time or binary size is tight: exprtk.hpp is about 46,800 lines (1.66 MB) of templates; the exprtk_disable_enhanced_features define cuts both but the readme warns it causes massive evaluation slowdowns
You compile expressions on a hot path: the readme says parser/symbol_table/expression construction and compilation are high-latency and must stay outside performance-critical code

You need peak throughput and can accept float or a JIT: the AsmJit-based muparserSSE (float) out-scored ExprTk in 5 of 8 2018 shootout runs and was faster on 5,580 of the 6,198 bench_expr_complete expressions it passed (derived from page data)
Function-call-heavy expressions where libm dominates: on bench_expr_random_with_functions the median gap shrinks to 1.2x over METL/FParser and 1.5x over muparser 2.2.4
You need a bug tracker: the GitHub repo is a mirror with no Issues tab and pull requests are closed rather than merged; support goes through the author's website

integration.dependencies: none (MPFR/GMP only if you instantiate it with an MPFR type)
integration.min_toolchain: C++98 (header declares min_cpp 199711L); readme lists GCC 3.5+, Clang 1.1+, MSVC 7.1+, Intel 8+, plus AMD, Nvidia, PGI, IBM XL, C++ Builder
integration.platforms: any (portable C++; no architecture-specific code paths)
integration.thread_safety: exprtk::parser is documented as non-thread-safe and non-copyable; compiled expressions hold references to symbol-table variables, so concurrent evaluation needs per-thread expression and variable instances (expressions must be recompiled from strings rather than copied); rebase of vector views during evaluation is undefined behaviour
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — same parse-once/evaluate-many model as muparser and binds C++ variables by pointer/reference, but a different API (symbol_table + parser.compile + expression.value) and a superset grammar; existing muparser call sites must be rewritten

gotchas: Structural bias in the cited shootout: ExprTk is hard-wired as the reference parser in src/ParserBench.cpp, so a rival whose result differs from ExprTk's is disqualified and scores 0 for that expression while ExprTk can never fail on accuracy, and the reference gets an extra untimed full pass before its ranked run. Re-counting the 2018 logs, this barely touched double-precision rivals (muparser 2.2.4 and METL 0 result mismatches, FParser at most 1; FParser's 67 losses on bench_expr_weird are parse errors); the mismatches fall on float builds, ExprTk's own ExprTkFloat about as often as muparserSSE.

The record's '1.18x on a single expression' understates the typical gap: re-parsing the committed 2018 bench_expr.txt log, muparser 2.2.4 is a median 3.4x slower per expression (range 1.05x to 15.8x, derived from page data); METL is a median 2.2x slower and wins 5 of 74 expressions
All published runs are 32-bit MSVC 2017 builds from 2018 against bundled 2013-2014 era rival versions (muparser 2.2.4, FParser 4.5); there are no 64-bit, GCC/Clang or current-muparser results

Object lifetimes are on you: variables, vectors, strings and functions registered in a symbol_table must outlive every compiled expression that references them, otherwise behaviour is undefined; compile() returns bool and errors must be checked via parser.error()
pick_this_over_siblings_when: None of the catalogued siblings (SLEEF, VDT, fmath, xsimd, NumKong) evaluate run-time expression strings; they speed up fixed compiled math kernels. Pick ExprTk when the formula is only known at run time; if it is known at compile time, write it in C++ and use SLEEF or fmath for the transcendental calls instead.
verified_claims_summary: In the author's math-parser-benchmark-project (32-bit MSVC 1913 Release, Intel Xeon E5-2687W @ 3.10 GHz, 2018 logs), pre-compiled ExprTk evaluated the 74 bench_expr.txt expressions 5,000,000 times each with a mean muparser-to-ExprTk speed ratio of 0.37-0.38 (about 2.7x) and a median per-expression slowdown for muparser 2.2.4 of 3.4x; across the eight 2018 suites muparser 2.2.4 scored 24-62 and the best double-precision rival (METL or FParser) 39-78 against ExprTk's 100.
status_note: The GitHub repo is a mirror of the author's site (header dated 20250101, last mirror commit 2025-01-01, PRs closed through 2026-07) and the benchmark logs stop in 2018, but the library is MIT, dependency-free, fuzzed on OSS-Fuzz per the readme, and copyable as a single header.
